title: What Medicines Actually Do Inside Your Body

chapters.title: The Lock and the Key
blocks: A pill is a pinch of powder. It has no eyes and no map. Yet it finds one specific target among the trillions of cells in your body.
Over the next ten minutes: six medicines, six tricks. Jam a lock. Cut an alarm wire. Replace a lost key. Forge a message. Run a fire drill. Break a wall.
Your cells talk with molecules. A signal drifts through your blood until it meets a receptor, a protein shaped to fit it.
Think of the receptor as a lock and the signal as a key. Right shape, the lock turns, and the cell does something.
Most medicines are fake keys. Some turn the lock. Some get stuck in it on purpose. And a few go after locks your body doesn't even own.
Quick note: this is how these drugs work, not advice on taking them. That decision belongs to you and your doctor.

chapters.title: Caffeine: The Key That Jams the Lock
blocks: Let's start with the drug most of you had today. Caffeine doesn't give you energy. It hides how tired you already are.
While you're awake, your brain burns fuel, and a by-product called adenosine slowly builds up between your neurons.
Adenosine fits into adenosine receptors. The more locks it fills, the stronger the pull toward sleep. Scientists call it sleep pressure.
Caffeine is shaped enough like adenosine to slide into those same receptors. But it doesn't turn the lock. It just takes the seat, and the sleepy signal can't get through.
Meanwhile, adenosine keeps piling up behind the blockade. When the caffeine fades, all that waiting sleep pressure lands at once.
And it fades slowly. A healthy adult clears about half of it in roughly five hours, so an afternoon coffee can still be working at bedtime.
For most healthy adults, the FDA cites four hundred milligrams a day as an amount not generally linked to harmful effects.
So that's trick number one: block a receptor. But what if the problem isn't a signal arriving, but a signal being made in the first place?

chapters.title: Ibuprofen: Cutting the Alarm Wire
blocks: Here's a strange fact. People took aspirin for about seventy years before anyone knew how it worked. In nineteen seventy-one, John Vane found the answer, and it explains ibuprofen too.
When you twist an ankle, damaged cells release a fatty acid. An enzyme called cyclooxygenase turns it into messengers called prostaglandins.
Prostaglandins are the alarm. They help the area swell and redden, and they make your pain nerves more sensitive, so every touch hurts more.
During an infection, prostaglandins also act on the part of your brain that sets your body temperature, and turn the thermostat up. That's a fever.
Ibuprofen slips into the enzyme's working pocket and blocks it. Fewer prostaglandins means less pain, less swelling, and a lower fever.
It doesn't heal the ankle. It turns down the alarm. And it doesn't stay long: your body clears about half of it in roughly two hours.
But there's a catch. This enzyme comes in two versions, and one of them makes prostaglandins that help protect your stomach lining.
Ibuprofen blocks both. That's why its label warns about stomach ulcers and bleeding.
The FDA also requires a warning about heart attack and stroke, a risk that rises with higher doses and longer use. Over the counter doesn't mean risk free.
Blocking works. But some diseases aren't about too much signal. They're about a key that's gone missing.

chapters.title: Insulin: Replacing a Lost Key
blocks: In January nineteen twenty-two, in a Toronto hospital, a teenage boy named Leonard Thompson was dying of type one diabetes.
Back then, that diagnosis was a death sentence. Doctors injected him with an extract from animal pancreas, and once they had purified it, his blood sugar came down.
That extract was insulin, and its discovery won Frederick Banting and John Macleod the Nobel Prize the very next year.
Here's what insulin does. After a meal, sugar from your food enters your blood. Beta cells in your pancreas sense it and release insulin.
Insulin is a key. It docks on receptors on your muscle and fat cells, and they pull sugar doors up to their surface. Sugar flows in, out of your blood.
In type one diabetes, the immune system destroys the beta cells. The key factory is gone, so sugar piles up in the blood instead of feeding the cells.
Insulin treatment replaces the missing key. It has to be injected, because insulin is a protein, and your stomach would digest it like food.
Since nineteen eighty-two, human insulin has been made by microbes carrying the human gene, the first medicine of that kind approved by the FDA.
Dosing is delicate: too much can push blood sugar dangerously low, so it's always managed with a doctor.
Insulin replaces a key. The next medicine is stranger. It forges a different message, one that gets your body to release its own insulin.

chapters.title: Mounjaro: The Forged Message
blocks: When food reaches your gut, it releases two hormones, GLP-1 and GIP. Their message is simple: food has arrived, get ready.
They nudge your pancreas to release insulin while sugar is rising. But your body tears them apart fast. Natural GLP-1 survives only about two minutes in the blood.
Mounjaro's active ingredient, tirzepatide, is a single molecule built to fit both locks: the GLP-1 receptor and the GIP receptor.
It also carries a fatty tail that grips albumin, a common protein in your blood. That shields it, so about half a dose is still around five days later.
That's why it's a once-a-week injection, instead of a hormone that vanishes in minutes.
In the pancreas, it boosts insulin release when blood sugar is high, and it lowers glucagon, the hormone that pushes sugar up.
In the stomach, it slows the exit, so food stays longer. And it acts on appetite, so people tend to eat less.
In a large trial, adults on the highest dose lost about twenty-one percent of their body weight on average, over seventy-two weeks. On placebo, about three.
Nausea and other stomach side effects are common, especially early on, and the label carries serious warnings. Who takes it, and at what dose, is a doctor's call.
The next medicine doesn't touch a lock at all. It writes instructions.

chapters.title: mRNA Vaccines: A Fire Drill for Your Immune System
blocks: Your immune system learns from experience. Usually it has to meet a germ, and survive it, before it knows that germ's shape. A vaccine is a rehearsal.
It shows your immune system a harmless piece of the enemy, so the first real meeting isn't the first meeting.
Older vaccines deliver that piece directly, as a weakened germ or a purified protein. A messenger RNA vaccine delivers a recipe instead.
The recipe is a strand of messenger RNA, wrapped in a tiny bubble of fat called a lipid nanoparticle, so it can slip into your cells.
Inside, your ribosomes, the cell's protein machines, read the recipe and build one piece of the virus. In the COVID vaccines, that was the spike protein.
The immune system sees that spike and learns its shape. It makes antibodies and trains T cells, without ever meeting the actual virus.
Then the cell breaks the recipe down. According to the CDC, it never enters the nucleus, where your DNA is kept, and it doesn't change your DNA.
For years, injected RNA set off inflammation. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman fixed that by swapping one RNA building block for a modified version. The alarm went quiet.
That work, first published in two thousand five, won them the Nobel Prize in twenty twenty-three.
Recommendations depend on age and health, and change over time. That's a question for your doctor.
A vaccine trains your own defenses. The last medicine skips the training and goes straight for the invader, through a lock your body doesn't have.

chapters.title: Antibiotics: Breaking a Wall You Don't Have
blocks: In nineteen twenty-eight, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on one of his bacteria plates had killed the bacteria around it.
He called it penicillin. Years later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team at Oxford turned it into a real medicine, and the three men shared a Nobel Prize.
Many bacteria wrap themselves in a wall made of a mesh called peptidoglycan. It's what keeps them from bursting.
To grow, they keep weaving new mesh, and enzymes stitch the strands together. Penicillin jams those stitching enzymes. It's a key that gets stuck for good.
Without the stitches, the wall weakens, water pushes in, and the bacterium bursts.
And your cells? They don't make peptidoglycan at all. The target only exists in the enemy. Scientists call that selective toxicity.
It also explains why antibiotics do nothing against colds or flu. Those are viruses, and viruses don't have that wall.
But bacteria evolve. Some make enzymes that cut penicillin apart before it can act. Every unnecessary dose gives those survivors a better chance to spread.
A large study in The Lancet estimated that in twenty nineteen, resistant bacteria directly caused about one point two seven million deaths worldwide.
That's why the standard advice is to take antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them, and exactly as prescribed.

chapters.title: One Idea, Six Tricks
blocks: So, six medicines, one idea. Caffeine jams a lock. Ibuprofen shuts down the machine that makes the alarm. Insulin replaces a missing key.
Mounjaro forges a hormone that lasts for days. A messenger RNA vaccine writes the recipe for a drill. And penicillin breaks a wall that only bacteria build.
None of it is magic: each one fits a shape that already exists. That's also why drugs have side effects. The same lock can sit in more than one place.
This channel is called Show Your Work for a reason: one idea, taken apart step by step. If you want the next one, subscribe, and I'll see you there.
